name: Erik Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play trumpet for a town band, record short horn cues for adverts and help an experienced brass tutor with beginners. I maintained buildings until five years ago and finished secondary school. I earn good fees because the band has many bookings, but I am still the junior player who needs a cue from the leader.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a booked season mean at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner and I have grown children, a mortgage and twelve months of expenses saved. Other bands work nearby, but I have not asked for a retirement-income estimate and I cannot spend a figure I do not know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that a quicker gig list helps if the written fee is still there. I would keep my eyes on the conductor rather than on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twelve months saved and a full paid calendar make one cancelled event manageable. Several other bands nearby also need trumpets from time to time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep paid band sets, horn cues and supervised beginner lessons. I use AI daily to sort practice clips, then listen to the source and play a sample before it reaches a learner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm in this picture. My own booked work still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an extra gig worth accepting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the written fee and finish time before booking transport. A late finish can use up a good fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you checked your future income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would request a written retirement estimate this winter and keep my band work while I read it.

I would watch the **conductor’s cues**, not a screen.

Request **written fees** and finish times before extra events.
Request a **written retirement estimate** this winter while keeping paid work.
feel: I feel **calm** about booked work and income.
S0.quote: A late finish can use up a good fee.
fieldNote: His **full calendar** and year of savings make a cancelled event tolerable.
Existing **daily AI sorting** is checked by listening and playing before learner use.

Request written retirement estimate this winter while keeping paid band work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band manager that generated horn cues could cut recording calls, but live players still need paid rehearsals. I would ask which studio and band hours are in the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert cues are nearly a third of my own pay. If clients use generated brass, I cannot assume the same band will add more paid nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask for three months of written paid band dates and a paid studio-engineer session on a new stem checker, a tool that separates notes in a recording. In the first year I would test it only on my own nameless trumpet take after approved local studio storage; I would compare every beat by ear with the original and stop if the timing changes or the file leaves the studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about recording fees. I like a new tool. I cannot make a client buy a recorded horn line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a pupil’s take be a test file?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A learner’s name and voice stay out of this tool; I own a clean practice take for testing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at a different band?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If paid horn or band calls actually fall, I would apply for a posted paid theatre brass seat only if my secondary schooling and experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the last bus gets me home; I would keep the current band until a signed offer. I would ask for written hours before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that AGI by 2028 could deliver an advert horn line overnight. I would ask venues to sign live dates and player fees before selling the season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the advert cue calls to stop in 2028, and some venues may use backing tracks instead of hiring the whole band. Playing robots arrive around 2031, three years later. A lost studio fee does not wait for a playing robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total cue invoices and request a signed paid band calendar. In the first year after 2028, if paid band nights fall too, I would apply for a posted community-centre brass assistant job only if my schooling and supervised teaching qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus still runs; I would keep current band and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about lost advert pay, but the twelve-month reserve and nearby bands give me time to search. I would be alarmed if most live dates disappeared as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you order new recording gear now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a signed paid client order covers it after band wages. I would keep nine months of expenses untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop work at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 60 in 2028, but I have not seen a written pension estimate. I would request one and keep paid calls until I know the figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band manager that five years until AGI by 2031 gives me time to learn live sound properly. I would want paid training before touching the venue’s mixing desk, the controls for loudness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert work might end by 2031 and playing robots might arrive around 2034. A sound-assistant job could fill the gap if I qualify, but a free certificate without wages would cost our household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would take a six-month live-sound course only if an actual venue offers a funded place, paid training hours and a timetable that fits the last bus without reducing my partner’s paid shifts. In the first year after 2031, if advert or band fees fall, I would apply for a posted paid sound-assistant role only if the certificate qualifies me, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and transport works; I would keep band and supervised pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious until the training leads to a real paid role. The year of savings lets me compare offers without pretending the course pays the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you mix a crowded show alone after training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The venue technician must supervise my first sound checks. I would not operate a crowded show alone until equipment and safety checks are signed off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course has free tuition but no paid hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep band bookings and ask for another intake. Free sound-course tuition still costs my partner and me time that could be paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that ten years until AGI by 2036 is time to put player fees and recording rights in writing. A leader cannot pay a player with a promise of future exposure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert calls may end by 2036 and playing robots could compete for live dates around 2039. We have twelve months saved and other local bands, but a written retirement estimate would tell me whether I can reduce nights later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would request a written retirement estimate and save ten percent of each extra paid horn session after mortgage, food and travel, aiming for sixteen months while leaving nine untouched. In the first year after 2036, if advert or live-band fees fall, I would apply for a posted theatre brass aide role only if my schooling qualifies, written net pay after travel covers lost fees and the last bus runs; I would keep paid band and pupil hours until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about a distant loss, because present bookings and savings hold. I would use the decade to get written terms rather than guess at retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra session pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I save nothing new from that source. Nine months stay untouched instead of becoming a course fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the band at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 in 2036, but I have no retirement date set. I would decide after seeing the written estimate and the paid calls available.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because advert calls could end before I know whether venue bookings will hold. Signed band dates, a qualified paid role and transport home would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the learner’s recording after class. A useful tool still needs a door that closes on private voices.

headlineQuote: A useful tool still needs a door that closes on private voices.
portrait: At **58**, Erik is a junior trumpeter who moved from building maintenance and completed secondary school.
His higher **musician pay**, twelve-month reserve and several local bands support present security.
He uses **AI daily** but tests a new stem checker only after paid instruction, approved local storage and ear checks.
A **funded sound course** needs a real paid place, transport and no lost partner wages before a qualified posted role.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase advert sessions before he knows whether paid band nights remain.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed band dates**, a qualified paid role with written net pay and transport home would help Erik.
